exam: A 30‑year‑old woman with a fractured femur is scheduled for emergency surgery. The operating theatre lacks a dedicated sharps container. What should you do? — Ensure a puncture‑resistant container is available or use a makeshift sealed container; do not reuse needles.
A patient with known HIV is undergoing laparotomy. Which precaution is added? — Add airborne precautions if the patient has active TB; otherwise maintain standard precautions.
During a routine hand‑washing, you notice a colleague’s gloves are torn. What is the immediate step? — Replace gloves immediately and report the incident to infection control.
A needle stick occurs during suturing. What is the first action? — Wash the area, apply antiseptic, report the injury, and consider post‑exposure prophylaxis.

In a low‑resource setting, a patient’s blood culture is unavailable. How do you decide on antibiotic prophylaxis for surgery? — Use local antibiogram data and standard surgical prophylaxis guidelines; if uncertain, choose broad‑spectrum agents with low resistance.
A surgical instrument shows a faint smear of blood. What is the correct handling? — Disinfect or sterilise the instrument before reuse; do not rely on visual inspection alone.

A patient with a history of hepatitis B is scheduled for elective surgery. What additional precaution is necessary? — Use standard precautions; if the patient is infectious, consider adding contact precautions and ensure all staff are vaccinated.
ai.title: Universal Precautions in Surgery
ai.subject: Surgery
ai.summary: Universal Precautions treat every patient as potentially infectious, guiding hand‑washing, PPE, and safe handling of sharps to prevent transmission of blood‑borne pathogens, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Use of gloves, masks, eye protection
sections.p: Universal Precautions are a set of practices that assume all patients may carry transmissible infections. They are not a diagnosis but a protocol applied to every surgical encounter.
Not applicable – the concept is a preventive measure, not a disease with stages.
The main risk is exposure to blood or body fluids that may contain HIV, HBV, HCV, TB, or other pathogens common in East Africa.
No clinical presentation; the focus is on preventing transmission during surgical care.
No investigations are required to establish Universal Precautions; however, awareness of local infection prevalence guides implementation.

sections.p: Failure to follow Universal Precautions can lead to occupational exposure, seroconversion, and outbreaks.

b: Hand hygiene before and after patient contact
Glove use for all invasive procedures
Mask and eye protection for splashes
Instrument sterilisation with autoclave or chemical methods
sections.p: Implement the protocol consistently: wash hands, wear gloves, use eye protection, discard sharps in puncture‑resistant containers, and clean instruments properly.

b: Post‑exposure prophylaxis for HIV if indicated
sections.p: After exposure, report and follow occupational health guidelines; monitor for seroconversion. Prevention relies on strict adherence and staff training.
Universal Precautions are often mixed up with Standard Precautions (which include additional measures for airborne and contact infections).
A negative HIV test does not guarantee absence of infection; window period may yield false negatives. Similarly, a negative HBV surface antigen may miss occult infection.

whenToSeekHelp: Needle stick injury with unknown HIV status
Exposure to blood from a patient with known HIV or HBV
Failure to adhere to precautions leading to outbreak
